summary: A heart with two ventricular septal defects (VSDs): a perimembranous defect high in the septum just below the aortic valve, and a muscular defect lower down in the trabecular septum, seen through windows cut into both ventricles. The lungs lie alongside, and the coronary arteries (red) and cardiac veins (blue) run on the surface.
clinical: Left ventricular pressure is several times right ventricular pressure, so blood shunts from the left to the right ventricle through a VSD, giving a harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border. Small defects are loud but harmless. Large ones flood the lungs and cause heart failure in infancy; left untreated they lead to pulmonary hypertension and eventually shunt reversal with cyanosis (Eisenmenger syndrome).

VSD is the most common congenital heart defect recognised at birth. Many small muscular VSDs close on their own as the muscle grows. Perimembranous defects close less often, and one lying just below the aortic valve can let an aortic cusp prolapse into it, causing aortic regurgitation; larger defects are closed surgically or with a catheter device.

Default13 01.name: Right heart and ventricular septum
Default13 01.description: Right atrium with the superior and inferior venae cavae, right ventricle opened by an anterior window, and the pulmonary trunk dividing into the pulmonary arteries. Its medial wall is the interventricular septum, which carries both defects: a round muscular VSD low in the trabecular septum, seen through the window, and a perimembranous VSD high up beside the tricuspid valve, just below the aortic valve.

Default15.name: Left heart and aorta
Default15.description: Left atrium receiving the four pulmonary veins, left ventricle opened by an anterior window, and the aorta: ascending aorta, arch with the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, and descending aorta. Because the left ventricle generates much higher pressure, a VSD shunts blood from here into the right ventricle.

Default copy2.name: Heart valves
Default copy2.description: The tricuspid and mitral valves with their chordae tendineae, the aortic valve joined to them through the fibrous skeleton, and the separate pulmonary valve in front. The membranous septum lies just below the aortic valve and beside the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve, which is why perimembranous VSDs sit here.
structures: Posterior leaflet of left atrioventricular valve

Default copy1.name: Coronary arteries
Default copy1.description: The right coronary artery in the right atrioventricular groove and the left coronary artery's anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) and circumflex branches, with diagonal branches. The anterior interventricular artery's septal branches supply the anterior two-thirds of the ventricular septum.

Default.name: Cardiac veins
Default.description: The cardiac veins, drawn in blue, running alongside the coronary arteries: the great cardiac vein beside the anterior interventricular artery drains into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium.

Default1.name: Lungs
Default1.description: The right and left lungs, drawn slimmed down beside the heart. A large VSD sends too much blood through the pulmonary circulation, and years of this overload remodel the pulmonary arterioles and cause pulmonary hypertension.

notes: The two VSDs are holes in the septal wall of the 'Default13 01' mesh, not separate parts, so they cannot be selected on their own. The muscular VSD is clear (round hole low in the septum, visible through the right ventricular window). The perimembranous VSD was placed from the creator's description and the septal openings high up near the tricuspid valve; several openings meet there where the right-heart mesh joins the valves, so which one is the defect is my best reading, not certain. The left-heart mesh ('Default15') is open on its septal side; the septum belongs to the right-heart mesh. The valve mesh is two pieces: the pulmonary valve, and the tricuspid, mitral and aortic valves joined together; valve identities are from their positions. The lungs look narrow from the front; they appear to be deliberately slimmed rather than cut. Colours: the importer reads vertex colours as linear, so the vertex-coloured heart halves render paler pink than the dark red myocardium in the creator's thumbnail. They were not overridden because each half also contains the white great vessels (the vertex colours blend from vessel to muscle), and one flat colour would paint the aorta red. The cardiac veins are a single uniform colour, so they were set to the thumbnail's navy.
